---
title: "Search Autocomplete Under a Strict Latency Budget"
description: "Advanced interview case: derive the principle, prove assumptions, and run small code."
---

## Interview challenge

When a user types 'sys', the system should suggest useful query completions. You have millions of search terms, a target response time of tens of milliseconds, and continuously changing popularity. Do you scan all terms on every keystroke?

No. The interesting design questions are **precomputation, ranking consistency, and staleness**, rather than the syntax of a trie.

## A simple prefix index

For each known query $w$, index every prefix of $w$ to a count or a bounded list of popular completions. A prefix lookup retrieves candidates instead of scanning the complete dictionary.

~~~ts
const index = new Autocomplete();
index.record('system design');
index.record('system design');
index.record('systems');
index.suggest('sys',2); // ['system design','systems']
~~~

This is the actual original implementation in the shared lab. Use POST /lab/search/record to build counts and GET /lab/search/suggest?prefix=sys to read suggestions.

## Understand the cost

If a term has length $|w|$, creating all prefixes requires $O(|w|)$ prefix entries (but naive string slicing can add character-copying cost). Maintaining the full set of words for every prefix can consume large memory. A production version keeps only top $K$ suggestions per prefix or uses a compact trie and a separate ranking store.

$$
\operatorname{Suggest}(p)=
\operatorname{TopK}_{w:\,p\preceq w}(\operatorname{score}(w)).
$$

Here $p\preceq w$ means that $p$ is a prefix of $w$.

## The harder interview twist

You want popular recent suggestions, not all-time counts. A frequency-only index becomes stale: yesterday's breaking query may remain ranked too high. A simple decayed score is

$$
S(w,t)=\sum_{e\in\mathrm{queries}(w)}e^{-\gamma(t-t_e)}
$$

for historical query events at times $t_e\leq t$, with decay rate $\gamma>0$. This is an illustrative scoring model, not code implemented by the small lab.

Update the index asynchronously, then serve a known version of the top-K prefix lists. You need a clear contract for indexing delay and what happens when a prefix has no cached candidates.

## Privacy, abuse and correctness

Raw user queries may contain names, emails and secrets. Popularity telemetry can become a privacy problem; apply retention, filtering and aggregation policies. Offensive or prohibited strings may need filtering before publication, not just after ranking.

## Tough follow-up

A million users search the same prefix in one second. The prefix index still has one hot key. Cache and replicate the already-computed top-K response; do not repeatedly recompute full suggestions from the entire term corpus.

## Mathematical Abstraction

$$
\mathrm{Memory}_{\mathrm{naive}}\propto\sum_{w\in W}|w|,
\qquad
\operatorname{latency}(p)\approx
T_{\mathrm{lookup}}+T_{\mathrm{topK}}.
$$

These are high-level cost models; precise memory and latency depend on the chosen index layout, cache hit rate and update method.
